a: There was a man named Ananias
p: Luke sets this story right after Barnabas' gift. The two scenes are meant to be read side by side.
b: The chapter break hides the link. Acts 4 ends with Barnabas, who sold a field and set the money "at the feet of the apostles" (4:36–37). Chapter 5 opens with "But" in Greek: Ananias does the same thing on the outside. The contrast is the point. Barnabas' gift was whole and honest; Ananias' gift was a show. His name, Hebrew Chananyah, means "the LORD has been gracious," which makes the story sadder. He is not the Ananias of Damascus (9:10) or the high priest Ananias (23:2).

a: He kept back some of the money for himself
p: The rare Greek verb is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for Achan, who stole from what was devoted to God.
b: The verb nosphizomai means to skim off or embezzle something entrusted to you. Paul uses it for slaves stealing from their masters (Titus 2:10). Its best-known use in the Greek Old Testament is Joshua 7:1, where Achan "kept back" some of the plunder from Jericho that belonged to God. Israel had just entered the land, and one man's secret theft brought death on him and trouble on the whole people. Many readers think Luke chose the word on purpose: the new community has just begun, and its first inside sin is a hidden theft from what was given to God, with the same deadly result.

a: how did Satan come to fill your heart
p: Luke used the same picture for Judas. The danger to the church now comes from the inside.
b: In Luke's first volume Satan "entered into Judas" (Luke 22:3), and in John the devil put the betrayal into Judas' heart (John 13:2). Peter's question puts Ananias in that line. Earlier in Acts the believers were "filled with the Holy Spirit" (4:31); here Satan has "filled" a heart. The same idea, with a related verb (plēroō here, pimplēmi in 4:31), makes the contrast. Peter does not excuse Ananias because Satan was involved: the next verse asks why he planned this in his heart. Satan prompts, but the person chooses.

a: The land was yours as long as you kept it, wasn't it?
p: Peter says the sale was voluntary. The sin was the lie, not keeping some money.
b: This verse matters for how the sharing in 2:44–45 and 4:32–35 is read. Peter says the land stayed Ananias' own, and even after the sale the money was his to decide about. Giving everything was not a rule of the church. Ananias could have given half and said so. His sin was pretending that a part was the whole, to win the honor Barnabas had won. Readers who see the shared life as a binding model for all Christians, and readers who see it as a free, Spirit-led moment, both appeal to this verse; it plainly makes the giving voluntary.

a: It was not people you lied to. It was God.
t: Lying to the Spirit is lying to God
p: Verse 3 says he lied to the Holy Spirit; verse 4, to God. Many read this as a witness to the Spirit's divinity.
b: Peter says first "you lied to the Holy Spirit" (5:3), then "you lied to God." Readers since the early church have taken this as one of the clearest places where the New Testament treats the Holy Spirit as God himself, and as a person who can be lied to, not only a force. Writers in the fourth-century debates over the Spirit's divinity used the two verses together. Others answer that the Spirit is called God here only as God's own presence and power, as when Israel was said to grieve God's Holy Spirit in the wilderness (Isaiah 63:10). A Where Christians differ card on the chapter page sets out the churches' answers. Peter's own point is simpler: the apostles are only men, so a lie told in the church is told to God.

p: A rare word, used in the New Testament only for Ananias, Sapphira and Herod Agrippa.
b: The verb ekpsychō means "breathe out (the soul or life)," and so "die." The New Testament uses it only three times: for Ananias here, for Sapphira (5:10), and for King Herod Agrippa, struck down by an angel because he did not give glory to God (12:23). The shared word links the three as deaths that come straight from God's judgment. The Greek Old Testament has it too (Ezekiel 21:7, Greek 21:12). Greek medical writers used it of fainting and of dying; it does not by itself say how death came.

p: Probably just the younger members of the church, though some see a recognized group.
b: Luke calls them "the younger men" here and "the young men" in 5:10. Some scholars have suggested an organized group of junior members, the counterpart of the elders, with tasks like burying the dead. Most think Luke simply means the able-bodied young men who were present. Burial on the same day was normal in Jewish Jerusalem, where the climate and purity rules made quick burial necessary (compare Deuteronomy 21:23). What is unusual is that Sapphira is not told, which shows how fast and how quietly it happened.

a: put the Lord's Spirit to the test
t: Testing God, as in the wilderness
p: "Testing" God was Israel's sin in the wilderness: seeing how far he would let them go.
b: In the Old Testament, to "test" God means to push him, to see whether he will act or whether he notices. Israel did this at Massah (Exodus 17:2, 7), and Deuteronomy 6:16 forbids it; Jesus quotes that law to the devil (Matthew 4:7). Peter accuses the couple of the same thing: they agreed together to see whether the Spirit, who lives in the church, would notice their lie. The wilderness echoes run through Acts 5–7 and come out in the open in Stephen's speech (7:39–43).

a: Right then she dropped at his feet, and her life left her
t: How to read the two deaths
p: Was this God's judgment, a death from shock, or a church disciplining itself? Readers differ.
b: Judgment from God. Most readers, ancient and modern, take the deaths as God's act. Peter does not curse Ananias; he only exposes the lie. With Sapphira he foretells her death, but even then it is God who acts. Shock. Some modern readers suggest Ananias collapsed from shock or shame, and Sapphira from hearing of her husband's death. The text gives no natural cause and treats both deaths as a sign. A founding warning. Many compare Achan (Joshua 7) and Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1–2): at the start of a new stage in God's dealings, a sin against holiness is punished severely as a warning. The Community Rule from Qumran punished a member who lied about his property with a year's exclusion and reduced food, a useful contrast. Luke says nothing about the couple's eternal fate, and many interpreters stress that.

p: In the oldest manuscripts this is the first time Acts calls the believers ekklēsia, "church."
b: The Greek ekklēsia means an assembly, a people called together. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates Hebrew qahal, the assembly of Israel, and Stephen will use it that way of Israel at Sinai (7:38, "the assembly in the wilderness"). The critical text has it here for the first time in Acts; the Byzantine text and the KJV already have it at 2:47. It is striking that the word first appears in a story about fear and judgment: the gathered people of God is holy, and God's presence in it is dangerous to lies.

p: A long roofed colonnade along the east side of the temple's outer court.
b: Josephus describes a colonnade on the east side of the temple courts, believed to go back to Solomon's time (Antiquities 20.221). It was a covered walkway open on one side, where teachers gathered pupils and crowds could stand in the shade. Jesus walked there in winter (John 10:23), and the crowd ran there after the healing of the lame man (3:11). Meeting there kept the first believers in the public eye, inside Israel's holiest place. They had not left the temple; they were teaching in it.

p: The Greek does not say who "the rest" were. The answer changes how verses 13 and 14 fit together.
b: Verse 13 says no one "of the rest" dared join them; verse 14 says more and more people were added. Readers have solved the tension in several ways. Outsiders: the general public admired the apostles but kept their distance after the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, though many still came to faith. Other believers: no ordinary believer dared to stand with the apostles in their place of leadership. Leaders or the rich: some suggest the rulers or the well-off held back. The first reading is the most common. The verb kollaō means "stick to, attach oneself to," a close bond.

a: his shadow at least would pass over some of them
p: Many ancient people thought a shadow carried a person's power. Luke reports the hope, not a promise.
b: In the ancient world a shadow was often thought to carry a person's power, for good or harm. The verb here, episkiazō "overshadow," is the one Luke uses for the Spirit's power coming on Mary (Luke 1:35) and the cloud at the transfiguration (Luke 9:34). Luke reports what people hoped, not a promise. The next verse says all were healed, and some readers take that to include the shadow; others note that Luke does not say so. Similar scenes surround Jesus' tassel (Mark 6:56) and Paul's handkerchiefs (19:11–12). The Western text adds that people were in fact set free from their illnesses (see the variant).

p: The priestly ruling class, who denied the resurrection the apostles kept preaching.
b: The Sadducees were the party of the high-priestly families and the Jerusalem aristocracy. Josephus says they rejected the resurrection and any teaching beyond the written law (Antiquities 18.16–17), and Acts says the same (23:8). The apostles were "declaring that in Jesus there is resurrection from the dead" (4:2), right in the temple the Sadducees ran. The word for "party" is hairesis, a school or sect, not yet "heresy": Acts uses it for the Pharisees (15:5; 26:5) and for the believers themselves, "the sect of the Nazarenes" (24:5, 14; 28:22). In Acts the Sadducees are the main opponents; the Pharisees are sometimes defenders (5:34; 23:9).

p: The Greek word zēlos can mean admirable zeal or bitter jealousy.
b: Zēlos is the root of "zeal." In Jewish tradition zeal for God's law was praised: Phinehas (Numbers 25:11–13) and Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2:24–26) were heroes of zeal, and Paul calls himself zealous for God before his call (22:3; Galatians 1:14). It can also mean envy at another's success, as when the leaders see the crowds following the apostles (compare 13:45; 17:5). Luke probably means both: the high priest saw himself defending God's house, but his anger was also envy of the apostles' popularity.

a: the doors of the prison were opened by an angel of the Lord
p: Greek stories also told of gods opening prison doors. Luke's three prison escapes have a shape readers would know.
b: Acts has three prison escapes: here, Peter in 12:6–11, and Paul and Silas in 16:25–26. Greek readers knew such scenes. In Euripides' play The Bacchae (405 BC), the god Dionysus' followers are jailed, and their chains fall off and the doors open "without a human hand." Some scholars, such as Richard Pervo, see Luke borrowing a stock literary scene; others note that the Old Testament has its own rescues (Daniel 6) and that Luke's escapes have a purpose, not just a thrill: the apostles are sent straight back to preach. A shared form does not settle what happened. Here the escape is told briefly, almost in passing, and the leaders cannot explain it (5:23–24).

p: The angel calls the message itself "this life," the new life that comes through the risen Jesus.
b: The Greek says "all the words of this life." Some read it as a Hebrew-style phrase meaning "these life-giving words." More likely "this life" names the message itself, as if it were a capital-L Life: the life that comes from the risen one, whom Peter has called "the Founder of life" (3:15). Jewish teachers called the Torah a source of life (Deuteronomy 32:47); the angel sends the apostles into the temple to speak of a new source. Paul calls it "the word of life" (Philippians 2:16).

a: the full council of elders of the Israelites
p: Luke may mean one body (the Sanhedrin, that is, the elders) or two bodies meeting together.
b: The Greek says they called "the Sanhedrin and all the council of elders (gerousia) of the sons of Israel." Most scholars read the "and" as "that is": Luke explains the Hebrew-sounding Sanhedrin with the Greek word his readers knew. Others think a wider body of elders was called in beside the regular court. The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's ruling council under the high priest, made up of priests, elders and scholars of the law; its exact makeup in the first century is debated, because the Mishnah's picture comes from later. The phrase "council of elders of the sons of Israel" echoes Exodus 12:21 in the Greek.

p: A senior priest who ran the temple police, second in rank to the high priest.
b: The Greek stratēgos tou hierou is the officer in charge of the Levites who guarded the temple. Many scholars identify him with the segan, the deputy of the high priest named in later Jewish sources, though the match is not certain. Josephus names a temple commander, Ananus, in the early 50s (Antiquities 20.131). His guards (5:22, 26) were temple police, not Roman soldiers. That is why they could not use force in front of a crowd that admired the apostles.

a: making us answer for this man's blood
p: The high priest fears being blamed for Jesus' death. Matthew's crowd had said, "His blood on us."
b: To "bring someone's blood on" a person is to make him guilty of a death (2 Samuel 1:16; Jeremiah 26:15). The high priest will not even say Jesus' name: "this man." He hears the apostles' preaching as an accusation, and in part it is (2:23; 3:15; 5:30). Matthew's Gospel has the crowd say before Pilate, "His blood on us, and on our children!" (Matthew 27:25). That verse was later misused to blame all Jews of every age. Acts shows something narrower and very human: a leader who does not want to be held responsible, and apostles who say the guilty can still repent (5:31).

a: Obeying God has to come before obeying people
p: Peter repeats what he said in 4:19. Greek readers would hear Socrates on trial.
b: This is the second time Peter refuses the council's order (see 4:19–20). The verb peitharcheō means to obey someone in authority. Greek readers would hear an echo of Socrates, who told the Athenian jury, "I will obey the god rather than you" (Plato, Apology 29d). Jewish martyrs said much the same to King Antiochus (2 Maccabees 7:2, 30). The verse became a key text in Christian thinking about conscience and the state: obedience to rulers is normal (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17), but when a ruler forbids what God commands, God comes first. Note that Peter disobeys only the ban on preaching; the apostles still appear when summoned and accept the beating.
r: 4:19–20; 5:40–41; Daniel 3:16–18; Daniel 6:10; 2 Maccabees 7:2; 2 Maccabees 7:30; Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17

a: by hanging him on a tree
p: Peter calls the cross a "tree," the word of Deuteronomy 21. Jews of that time already linked that law to crucifixion.
b: The law in Deuteronomy says that the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree must be buried before night, "for a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23). Jewish writers before Jesus applied this law to crucifixion: the Temple Scroll from Qumran (column 64) and the Nahum Pesher (4Q169) speak of hanging people alive on a tree. So when Peter says "tree" (xylon, wood), the leaders would hear the charge that Jesus died under God's curse. Peter's answer is that God raised him: the curse was overturned. Acts uses the word again in 10:39 and 13:29; Paul and Peter's letter build on it (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24).

p: Archēgos is a leader who goes first and opens the way for others. English Bibles render it many ways.
b: Archēgos combines "first" or "beginning" with "lead." It can mean a ruler or prince, the founder of a city or family, or a champion who goes ahead of his people. Peter used it in 3:15, "the Founder of life," and this translation keeps that rendering. Hebrews calls Jesus the archēgos of salvation and of faith (Hebrews 2:10; Hebrews 12:2). Moses is called a "ruler" (archōn) and "redeemer" in Stephen's speech (7:35), a close parallel: the leader God sent whom his people rejected. The phrase "to his right hand" can also be read "by his right hand," meaning by God's power.

p: One of the most honored teachers of his day, remembered in the Mishnah and, in Acts, as Paul's teacher.
b: Rabban Gamaliel, later called "the Elder," was a leading Pharisee teacher in Jerusalem in the 30s. Jewish tradition makes him a grandson of the great teacher Hillel. The Mishnah says that "when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased" (Sotah 9:15). Paul says he was trained "at the feet of Gamaliel" (22:3). His presence shows that the Sanhedrin included Pharisees as well as the Sadducee priests, and that Pharisees could act as a brake on the priests (compare 23:6–9). Later Christian legend made him a secret believer (Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 1.65–66), and the priest Lucian's account of finding Stephen's body (AD 415) has Gamaliel say he buried Stephen in his own tomb and was buried there himself. Those stories are not history.

p: Josephus dates a rebel named Theudas about ten years after this speech. Scholars disagree on how to explain it.
b: Josephus tells of Theudas, a man who claimed to be a prophet and led a large crowd to the Jordan, promising to divide the river. The governor Fadus (about AD 44–46) sent cavalry, killed many, and cut off his head (Antiquities 20.97–98). That is about ten years after Gamaliel's speech, and Gamaliel puts Theudas before Judas the Galilean (AD 6). Views: another Theudas, an earlier rebel of the same common name, perhaps one of the many uprisings after Herod's death in 4 BC; Luke's mistake, misdating a rebel he knew of; Luke used Josephus and misread him, since Josephus mentions Judas' sons right after Theudas (20.102). The last view requires Acts to be written after AD 93; most scholars doubt Luke read Josephus. The chapter page gives the details.

a: Judas the Galilean appeared at the time of the registration
t: Judas the Galilean and the census
p: When Rome counted Judea's people for tax in AD 6, Judas called it slavery and led a revolt.
b: In AD 6 Augustus removed Herod's son Archelaus and made Judea a Roman province. The governor of Syria, Quirinius, carried out a registration of people and property for tax (Luke 2:2 mentions a census under Quirinius; how the two relate is debated). Josephus says Judas from Gamala ("the Galilean") urged the Jews not to pay, saying that only God was their master, and that he founded a "fourth philosophy" alongside the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes (War 2.118; Antiquities 18.1–10, 23). Josephus does not report how Judas died; Gamaliel says he perished. His sons were crucified in the 40s (Antiquities 20.102). The Byzantine text and the KJV add that he drew away many people (laon hikanon, KJV "much people"); the older text has just "people."

p: Gamaliel's verb is the one the false witnesses will use about the temple in 6:14.
b: The verb katalyō means to pull down or dissolve. Gamaliel says a merely human movement will be "torn down"; God's cannot be. In the next chapter the same verb returns in the charge against Stephen: Jesus "will tear down this place" (6:14), the charge brought against Jesus himself (Matthew 26:61). This translation uses "tear down" in all these places so the link can be seen. The irony is Luke's: the leaders who fear that Jesus will tear down the temple are themselves at risk of trying to tear down God's work.

p: One Greek word, theomachoi, used in Greek tragedy and in 2 Maccabees for those who resist a god.
b: Gamaliel's word theomachos means "God-fighter." Euripides uses the verb for King Pentheus, who resisted the god Dionysus and was destroyed (Bacchae 45). The martyrs in 2 Maccabees warn the persecuting king that he is setting out "to fight against God" (2 Maccabees 7:19). Gamaliel's test, wait and see whether it lasts, has a later Jewish parallel: "Every gathering that is for the sake of Heaven will last in the end" (Mishnah Avot 4:11). Readers take Gamaliel's advice in two ways: as real openness, or as a cautious leader's way to avoid trouble. Either way, Luke's readers know the answer: the movement did last.

p: Probably the synagogue punishment of up to thirty-nine lashes. Jesus had warned of this.
b: The verb derō means to skin or flog. The punishment was probably the one in Deuteronomy 25:1–3, which allowed up to forty blows; Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine to avoid going over by mistake (Mishnah Makkot 3:10–11; Paul received it five times, 2 Corinthians 11:24). It was a disciplinary beating for members of the community, painful and shaming. Jesus had told his followers, "They will hand you over to councils and whip you in their synagogues" (Matthew 10:17). This is the first time in Acts that believers suffer bodily harm.

a: found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name
p: Luke puts "counted worthy" next to "dishonored": a deliberate paradox.
b: The verbs stand side by side in Greek: katēxiōthēsan ("they were counted worthy," a word of honor) and atimasthēnai ("to be dishonored"). In a culture of honor and shame, a public beating was a disgrace; the apostles count it an honor. Jesus had said, "Be glad and celebrate, because your reward in heaven is great. People persecuted the prophets who lived before you in the same way" (Matthew 5:12). "The Name" with no other word is striking: Jews said "the Name" (ha-Shem) to avoid speaking God's own name, and here it means the name of Jesus (compare 3 John 7).

p: The first believers met in two places: the temple courts and private homes.
b: Luke's phrase kat' oikon means "at home" or "house by house"; he uses it for the breaking of bread in homes in 2:46 too. The temple gave them a public place to teach; homes were where they ate together, prayed and taught their own. For three centuries most Christian meetings were in houses; the first known church building, at Dura-Europos in Syria, was a converted house of the 230s. The two settings also show how Luke sees the first believers: still faithful worshipers at the temple, and also a new family gathering at home.

p: Probably Jewish believers whose language was Greek, and Jewish believers who spoke Aramaic.
b: The word Hellēnistai is not found in Greek before Acts. It comes from a verb meaning "to speak Greek" or "live in the Greek way." Most scholars, following Martin Hengel, take the Hellenists to be Jews from the lands of the dispersion who had settled in Jerusalem and spoke Greek as their first language; the "Hebrews" were Jews of the land who spoke Aramaic (and read Hebrew). Both groups were Jewish: the first Gentile believers come only in chapters 10–11. A minority view (Henry Cadbury's) took the Hellenists to be Gentiles, but most now reject it, since 9:29 uses the same word for Greek-speaking Jews who tried to kill Paul. The language split meant separate synagogues (6:9), and probably separate worship and food lines.

p: The Greek word is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's grumbling against Moses.
b: Gongysmos is an imitative word, like "muttering." In the Greek of Exodus 16 and Numbers 11–17 it is Israel's complaint in the wilderness against Moses and God. Luke's readers would catch the echo: the new people of God faces an old temptation. But unlike Israel's grumbling, this complaint is about a real wrong, and the leaders listen and act. The apostles' answer, choosing helpers so that the leaders are not crushed by the work, recalls Moses taking Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:13–26) and the seventy elders who shared Moses' burden (Numbers 11:16–17).

p: Widows without family had no income. Many devout Greek-speaking Jews moved to Jerusalem to end their lives there.
b: The law of Moses commands Israel to care for the widow, the fatherless and the foreigner (Deuteronomy 14:28–29; Deuteronomy 24:19–21), and the prophets judge Israel by it (Isaiah 1:17). A widow with no son to support her could be destitute. Jews from the dispersion often moved to Jerusalem in old age to die and be buried near the temple, so there may have been many Greek-speaking widows far from their families. Later Jewish sources describe a daily soup kitchen and a weekly community chest for the poor (Mishnah Peah 8:7); whether those existed this early is uncertain. The church had its own daily serving, which the complaint shows was not reaching everyone.

t: Serving tables and serving the word
p: Luke uses one word family three times: the daily serving, serving tables, serving the word.
b: Diakonia (6:1, "serving"), diakoneō (6:2, "serve") and diakonia again (6:4, "serving the word") come from the family that later gives the church the word "deacon." Luke is not ranking table work below preaching; both are service. The point is division of labor. "Tables" may mean dining tables where food was handed out, or money tables, as with the money changers (Matthew 21:12), which would make the task the management of funds. The Seven are never called "deacons" (diakonoi) in Acts, and two of them, Stephen and Philip, are next seen preaching, not serving food.

a: seven men with a good name
p: Seven was a natural number for a council. Josephus says Jewish towns were run by seven men.
b: Josephus says Moses ordered that each city be governed by seven men (Antiquities 4.214), and that he himself appointed seven judges in each town of Galilee (War 2.571). Later rabbinic texts speak of "the seven good men of the town" who handled public affairs. So seven was a familiar size for a local council, and the number need not be symbolic. Some readers see seven as a number of completeness. Note that the whole community chooses the men, and the apostles appoint them (6:3, 6): both have a part, which churches with different forms of government have all appealed to.

p: The only one of the Seven whose city is named. He was a Gentile who had become a Jew.
b: A prosēlytos was a Gentile who had converted to Judaism, with circumcision for men. Nicolaus was born outside Israel, in Antioch of Syria, where Gentiles will first hear the gospel in large numbers (11:20). All seven names are Greek, which suggests that the men chosen came from the Hellenists' side, the side that had complained: a generous answer. Irenaeus later said the Nicolaitans of Revelation 2:6, 15 took their name from this Nicolaus (Against Heresies 1.26.3); Clement of Alexandria defended him and said his followers twisted his words (Stromata 3.4). Neither claim can be checked.

p: Not the apostle Philip, but one of the Seven, who will preach in Samaria and to the Ethiopian.
b: This Philip is not Philip of Bethsaida, one of the Twelve (1:13; John 1:43–44). He is the one Acts later calls "Philip the evangelist," who "was one of the Seven" and lived in Caesarea with four daughters who prophesied (21:8–9). He preaches in Samaria and baptizes the Ethiopian official (8:5–40). Early Christian writers sometimes mixed the two Philips up (Eusebius, Church History 3.31). Philip, like Stephen, shows that the Seven did far more than hand out food.

a: they prayed and laid their hands on them
t: Who laid hands on the Seven?
p: The Greek allows the apostles or the whole community. Churches have read it both ways.
b: The sentence moves from "they" (the community) presenting the men to the apostles to "they" praying and laying on hands. Most readers assume the apostles laid on hands, because verse 3 says "we will put them in charge"; Codex Bezae makes that explicit. But the grammar allows the whole community. Laying on hands is an Old Testament act of passing on a task and blessing: Moses on Joshua ("He laid his hands on him and gave him his orders," Numbers 27:23), and all Israel on the Levites (Numbers 8:10). In Acts it goes with healing, the giving of the Spirit and sending for a task (8:17; 13:3; 19:6; 28:8). Whether this is ordination to an office is the subject of the Where Christians differ card on this chapter.

a: the word of God kept growing
p: One of Luke's summary statements, which mark the stages of Acts.
b: Luke pauses at intervals to say that the word grew and the number of believers multiplied (6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:31). The phrases sound like Genesis ("be fruitful and multiply") and like Exodus 1:7, where Israel grows in Egypt in spite of Pharaoh. Here the growth comes right after a crisis is solved. It closes the section on the church in Jerusalem before Stephen's story opens the way out to Samaria and beyond. The word itself is pictured as a living, growing thing, like seed (Luke 8:11).

p: Ordinary priests, not the chief priests. There were thousands of them, and many were poor.
b: Jerusalem's priests were divided into twenty-four divisions that took turns serving in the temple (1 Chronicles 24:1–19; Luke 1:5, 8). Most were ordinary men who lived in Judean villages, far below the wealthy chief-priestly families who ran the temple and opposed the apostles. Josephus says that in the 50s the high priests' servants seized the tithes meant for ordinary priests, so that some of them starved (Antiquities 20.181). A "big crowd" of priests joining the believers shows that faith in Jesus did not mean leaving the temple. Some have guessed that Hebrews was written to such converted priests; that is only a guess.

p: Freedmen were former slaves. Many Jews taken to Rome as captives were later freed.
b: "Freedmen" translates Libertinoi, a Latin word. When Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, many Jews were taken to Rome as slaves and later freed; Philo says most of the Jews in Rome were freedmen (Embassy to Gaius 155). Their descendants could have founded a synagogue in Jerusalem. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 records that Theodotus son of Vettenus, priest and synagogue leader, built a synagogue "for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments," with rooms for visitors from abroad. Some scholars connect it with the Freedmen because Vettenus is a Roman name; that is possible but not proven. The grammar leaves open whether Luke means one synagogue or as many as five.

t: Claude's theory: was Saul in the room?
p: Saul of Tarsus came from Cilicia, studied in Jerusalem, and stands at Stephen's death.
b: This is my suggestion, not something the text says. Among Stephen's opponents are Jews "from Cilicia." Saul was from Tarsus, the chief city of Cilicia (21:39; 22:3), was living in Jerusalem as a student of Gamaliel, and appears at Stephen's death minding the witnesses' cloaks (7:58; 22:20). It would fit if Saul worshiped in the synagogue of the Cilicians and was among those who could not answer Stephen in debate (6:10). Many commentators have made the same guess. If so, the argument Saul lost to Stephen, about the temple, the law and a crucified Messiah, became his own message later.

a: blasphemous things against Moses and against God
p: Speaking against the law or the temple could count as speaking against God, who gave them.
b: In the strict sense, blasphemy was cursing God's name, and the punishment was stoning (Leviticus 24:10–16). The Mishnah later limits it to pronouncing the divine name itself (Sanhedrin 7:5), but in the first century the word could be used more loosely for insulting God's honor. Moses stands for the law God gave through him, so the charge pairs Moses with God. Jesus was charged with blasphemy too (Matthew 26:65). Luke says the accusers were planted and the witnesses lying (6:13), yet Stephen's speech will show that he did see the temple differently from his accusers.

a: against the holy place and the law
t: Charges like Jesus', and like Jeremiah's
p: Stephen faces the charge Jesus faced, and the charge Jeremiah faced long before.
b: Luke's Gospel leaves out the false witnesses at Jesus' trial who said he would destroy the temple (compare Mark 14:57–58 and Matthew 26:61). Luke saves that charge for Stephen. The Old Testament precedent is Jeremiah, who preached that God would make the temple like Shiloh: the priests and prophets said to the officials and to all the people, "The sentence for this man is death... He prophesied against this city" (Jeremiah 26:11). Jeremiah was spared; Stephen will not be. Speaking against the temple in God's name had a long and costly history in Israel.

p: The charge repeats words from Jesus' trial. In a sense Jesus had said something like it.
b: At Jesus' trial the witnesses said, "This man said, 'I am able to tear down God's sanctuary and build it in three days.'" (Matthew 26:61). John reports a saying behind the charge: "Tear this temple down, and within three days I will raise it" (John 2:19), which John explains as Jesus' body. Jesus also foretold the temple's ruin: "here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Matthew 24:2). So the charge was false as stated (Jesus would not destroy it himself), but it grew from something he said. If Luke wrote after AD 70, as most scholars think, his first readers knew that Rome had destroyed the temple; others date Acts about 62, before the fall (see the book's introduction).

a: the customs that Moses passed on to us
p: Luke often calls the Jewish law "the customs," the law as people actually lived it.
b: Ethos means custom, practice or way of life. Luke uses it for circumcision "as Moses' custom requires" (15:1), and for the charge that Paul taught Jews "not to live by the customs" (21:21); Paul answers that he did nothing against the ancestral ways, the same Greek word (28:17). The word points to the law as a way of life that marked Jews off from others: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, temple worship. To "change the customs" was to threaten Jewish identity itself, which explains the fury against Stephen.

a: it looked like an angel's face
p: Moses came down from Sinai with a shining face. Stephen, accused of speaking against Moses, looks like him.
b: The Old Testament says of Moses that "the skin of his face was shining from his speaking with him" (Exodus 34:29). Stephen is accused of speaking against Moses, and Luke shows him looking like Moses, glowing with God's presence. Angels were thought to shine (Luke 24:4; Matthew 28:3), and to have "the face of an angel" meant to look radiant and to come from God's presence (compare 1 Samuel 29:9, "as good as an angel of God," and 2 Samuel 14:17, "like God's angel," of goodness and wisdom). The judges see it, and judge him anyway.
r: Exodus 34:29–35; 1 Samuel 29:9; 2 Samuel 14:17; Matthew 17:2; Matthew 28:3; Luke 24:4; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18

p: Luke begins with a formal question from the high priest. The chapter ends with a mob.
b: The high priest's question gives Stephen a chance to answer the charges of 6:13–14, as in a trial. But the scene ends with a rush to stone him (7:57–58) and no verdict. Historians weigh this in two ways. Some see a lynching: under Roman rule, the Sanhedrin could not carry out death sentences without the governor (John 18:31), so a sudden stoning fits a crowd out of control. Others think the council did act, perhaps when Roman control was weak, for example after Pilate was removed in AD 36 or 37. The date of Stephen's death is usually put between about 31 and 36.

p: The longest speech in Acts. It is less a defense than a retelling of Israel's story, with a sharp ending.
b: Stephen answers the charge that he spoke against the temple and the law by retelling Israel's history from Abraham to Solomon. Three threads run through it. God met his people outside the land and the temple: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Midian and at Sinai. Israel repeatedly rejected the deliverers God sent: Joseph, then Moses. And God's dwelling is a tent that moves, not a house built by hands. The speech often follows the Greek Old Testament, and it differs from the Hebrew text in several places, which this page notes one by one. Whether Luke composed it or summarized a real speech is discussed on the chapter page.

a: While our father Abraham was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran
p: Genesis tells the call in Haran. Stephen places it earlier, in Mesopotamia, as other Jewish writers did.
b: Genesis tells of Terah taking Abram from Ur to Haran (Genesis 11:31) and then gives God's call (Genesis 12:1). Read in order, the call came in Haran. Stephen says God appeared to Abraham before Haran, in "Mesopotamia" (here meaning Ur of the Chaldeans, 7:4). He is not alone. Genesis itself has God say, "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 15:7), and Nehemiah 9:7 says the same. Philo (On Abraham 62–67) and Josephus (Antiquities 1.154) also put the first call in Chaldea. Stephen follows a reading of Genesis known in his day. His point: God first spoke to Israel's father in a pagan land.

p: A title from Psalm 29. Stephen begins and ends his speech with God's glory.
b: "The God of glory sends out thunder" (Psalm 29:3). Stephen opens his speech with the God of glory appearing to Abraham far from any temple, and the chapter ends with Stephen seeing "God's glory" in heaven (7:55). The frame matters: God's glory, which Israel associated with the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11), is not tied to one building. It appeared in Mesopotamia and it appears to Stephen outside the temple, in the place of his death.

t: Did Terah die before Abraham left?
p: Stephen says Abraham left after Terah died. The Hebrew numbers suggest Terah lived sixty more years.
b: Genesis says "Terah lived 70 years and fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran" (Genesis 11:26), that "Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran" (Genesis 12:4), and that "Terah's days came to 205 years, and Terah died in Haran" (Genesis 11:32). If Abram was born when Terah was 70, Terah was 145 when Abram left and lived another 60 years. Explanations: the Samaritan Pentateuch gives Terah 145 years at death, which fits Stephen exactly; Abram not the eldest, listed first for importance, and born when Terah was 130; Genesis' order: Genesis reports Terah's death (11:32) before the call (12:1), and Philo too says Abraham left after his father died (On the Migration of Abraham 177). Stephen follows that reading of the story.

a: not even room to plant a foot
p: The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 2:5. Abraham lived in the promised land as a guest.
b: In Deuteronomy God tells Israel not to take Edom's land: "not even room for the sole of a foot" (Deuteronomy 2:5). Stephen uses the same Greek phrase for Abraham. The father of Israel owned nothing in the promised land but a grave (Genesis 23), and lived there on a promise. Hebrews makes the same point: Abraham "lived in tents" in the land of promise, as a foreigner (Hebrews 11:8–10). For Stephen, God's people were a people of promise before they were a people with land or temple.

t: Four hundred years, or four hundred thirty?
p: Genesis 15 says four hundred; Exodus 12 says four hundred thirty. Both are in the Bible.
b: Stephen quotes Genesis 15:13 nearly word for word in its Greek form: four hundred years of slavery. Exodus says, "The Israelites had lived in Egypt for a span of four hundred and thirty years" (Exodus 12:40), and Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the law (Galatians 3:17). The Greek Old Testament of Exodus 12:40 counts the time in Canaan and in Egypt together. Most readers take four hundred as a round number. The difference was already discussed by ancient Jewish interpreters and is not a problem Stephen created.

p: Stephen joins Genesis 15:14 to Exodus 3:12, where God said Israel would serve him "on this mountain."
b: The first half of the verse is from Genesis 15:14. The second half recalls God's word to Moses at the burning bush: "you will all serve God on this mountain" (Exodus 3:12), meaning Sinai. Stephen says "in this place." His hearers had just used "this place" for the temple (6:13–14). Some readers think Stephen deliberately moves the promise from Sinai to the land, and so to Jerusalem; others think he means the land in general. Either way, the worship God promised was the goal of the exodus, and Stephen honors it.

p: Circumcision came with God's covenant with Abraham, centuries before Moses and the temple.
b: Genesis 17:9–14 gives circumcision as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his offspring, to be done on the eighth day. Stephen, accused of speaking against the customs of Moses (6:14), honors circumcision as God's own gift. He will later turn the word against his hearers: "uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears" (7:51). Paul makes a related argument about the order of events: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised (Romans 4:9–12). The question of circumcising Gentile believers will come to a head in Acts 15.

a: Out of jealousy the patriarchs sold Joseph away into Egypt
p: Stephen's story of Joseph is the first of two rejected deliverers. Moses is the second; Jesus, unnamed, is the third.
b: Stephen tells Joseph's story briefly but with a shape: his brothers turned on him from jealousy, God was with him, he became ruler, and in the end he saved the very brothers who sold him. The same word "jealousy" drove the high priest against the apostles (5:17). Moses' story will follow the same pattern even more plainly (7:23–36). Stephen does not draw the line to Jesus until 7:52, but his hearers could see where it was going. Christian writers from the second century on read Joseph as a figure of Christ.

p: The Hebrew counts seventy; the Greek and a Dead Sea Scroll count seventy-five. Stephen follows the Greek.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 46:27 says that all the persons of Jacob's house who came to Egypt "numbered seventy" (also Exodus 1:5; Deuteronomy 10:22). The Greek translation of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy-five, adding grandsons of Joseph listed in its version of Genesis 46:20. This is not a Greek invention alone: a Hebrew scroll of Exodus from Qumran (4QExod-b) also reads seventy-five at Exodus 1:5. So Stephen's number reflects a real form of the Old Testament text in use in his day. Different counts of who is included explain the gap; neither number is a slip.

a: the tomb Abraham had paid silver for, buying it from Hamor's sons at Shechem
p: Genesis says Abraham bought a cave at Hebron and Jacob bought land at Shechem. Stephen merges the two.
b: In Genesis, Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23:16–20), and Jacob was buried there (Genesis 50:13). Jacob bought land near Shechem: "He bought the piece of land where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, for a hundred qesitahs" (Genesis 33:19), and Joseph's bones were buried there (Joshua 24:32). Stephen names Abraham as buyer, Hamor's sons as sellers, Shechem as the place. Views: telescoping, a speaker compressing two purchases into one, as ancient retellings often did; an error, Luke's or Stephen's; a local tradition that the twelve patriarchs lay at Shechem (Jerome reports their tombs shown there; Josephus places the brothers at Hebron). Some, such as Martin Scharlemann, connect Stephen's interest in Shechem with Samaritan tradition. No solution removes the difference; the speech is honest to its sources rather than to a harmonized Genesis.

p: Stephen uses Pharaoh's own word from Exodus 1:10.
b: Pharaoh said to his people, "Come on, let us outsmart them, or they will multiply still more" (Exodus 1:10). The Greek Old Testament has the verb katasophizomai, "use cunning against," and Stephen uses it here. He adds that Pharaoh made the Israelites put their own babies out to die, which is his summary of Exodus 1:22: "Every son who is born, you must throw into the Nile." Stephen's word "put out" (ekthetos) is the Greek word for the exposure of unwanted infants, a practice his Greek-speaking hearers knew well.

a: a fine child in God's eyes
p: A Hebrew-style way of saying "exceptionally fine." It also says God had his eye on the child.
b: Exodus 2:2 says his mother "saw him, that he was good"; the Greek translation has asteios, "fine, lovely," the word here and in Hebrews 11:23. Stephen adds "to God." In Hebrew style, "to God" can be a way to say "very": Nineveh was "a great city to God," meaning an enormous city (Jonah 3:3). So the phrase may mean "an extraordinarily fine child." But the words also suggest that God himself saw something in him. Both readings are old, and English Bibles divide.

a: He had power in his words and in his actions
t: Moses: educated and powerful in speech
p: Exodus says nothing of Moses' schooling, and Moses called himself "heavy of mouth."
b: Exodus does not describe Moses' schooling. Jewish writers of Stephen's time filled the gap: Philo says Egyptian, Greek and other teachers taught him arithmetic, geometry, music and philosophy (Life of Moses 1.21–24). Stephen also says Moses was powerful "in his words," while in Exodus Moses protests, "I have never been a man of words... I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue" (Exodus 4:10). Readers resolve this in different ways: Moses' complaint was modesty or fear, not fact; "words" means what God later spoke through him; or Stephen draws on the tradition of Moses as a great figure. Luke says the same of Jesus, powerful in deed and word (Luke 24:19).

p: Stephen divides Moses' 120 years into three periods of forty. Jewish tradition did the same.
b: Exodus does not give Moses' age when he killed the Egyptian. It says he was eighty when he spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7), and Deuteronomy says he died at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7). Stephen gives forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian (7:30) and forty in the wilderness (7:36). The rabbis divided Moses' life the same way: forty years in Pharaoh's court, forty in Midian, forty serving Israel (Sifre on Deuteronomy 357). The word "go and see" (episkeptomai) is the verb used of God "visiting" his people to help them (Luke 1:68): Moses goes to his people as God's agent, though he does not know it yet.

p: Stephen adds a line that is not in Exodus: Moses expected his people to understand God's plan, and they did not.
b: Exodus says only that Moses was afraid when the killing became known (Exodus 2:14). Stephen gives Moses' inner thought: he expected his brothers to see that God was rescuing them through him. Their failure to understand is the heart of Stephen's case, and Luke's: the disciples failed to understand Jesus' sufferings (Luke 18:34; Luke 24:25), and Peter tells Jerusalem's people that when they acted against Jesus they did not understand what they were doing (3:17). Stephen's speech moves from not understanding to refusing (7:39, 51). The Greek word for "salvation" (sōtēria) is the word Luke uses for the salvation Jesus brings.

a: in the wilderness of Mount Sinai
p: Exodus says the bush was at Horeb and calls the angel "the angel of the LORD." Stephen says Sinai and "an angel."
b: Exodus places the burning bush at "God's mountain, toward Horeb" (Exodus 3:1); Horeb and Sinai are usually taken as two names for the same mountain. Exodus says "The angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blaze of fire" (Exodus 3:2), and then God himself speaks from the bush. Stephen keeps both: an angel appears (7:30, 35, 38) and the voice is the Lord's (7:31). The holy place is in the wilderness, far from Jerusalem, which suits Stephen's point that God is met wherever he chooses (7:33). The Byzantine text and the KJV read "an angel of the Lord" (see the variant).

a: the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob
p: Exodus 3:6 has "the God of your father," singular. Stephen has the plural, as in Exodus 3:15.
b: God said at the bush, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6). Stephen's Greek says "of your fathers," plural, the form God uses a few verses later (Exodus 3:15). Peter used the same title in the temple (3:13), and Jesus used this verse to prove the resurrection (Matthew 22:32). Exodus says Moses hid his face; Stephen says he trembled and did not dare to look closely.

a: The spot you are standing on is holy ground
p: Stephen is accused of speaking against the holy place. He points out that God made a desert place holy.
b: Stephen's accusers charged him with speaking "against the holy place" (6:13). He answers by reminding them of the first place in Israel's story that God called holy ground: a patch of desert at Sinai, outside the promised land, where there was no temple. Sacred space in the Bible is where God is present. Stephen does not deny that the temple was holy; he denies that God's holiness was limited to it. This verse is the turning point of the speech's argument about place.

p: Lytrōtēs, "redeemer," appears only here in the New Testament. Stephen gives Moses a title that points to Jesus.
b: The man in Egypt asked, "Who put you in charge as ruler and judge?" (7:27, from Exodus 2:14). Stephen answers that God sent Moses as "ruler and redeemer." Lytrōtēs is used in the Greek Psalms of God himself (Psalm 19:14; Psalm 78:35). On the road to Emmaus two disciples say they had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel (Luke 24:21), and Peter called Jesus "Founder and Savior" (5:31). The parallel is clear: the man the people pushed away was the very one God sent to rescue them. The verb "disowned" (arneomai) is the one Peter used of the people's rejection of Jesus before Pilate (3:13–14).

p: Stephen's Greek says "the Red Sea," as the Greek Old Testament does. The Hebrew name means "Sea of Reeds."
b: The Hebrew name of the sea Israel crossed is Yam Suf, "Sea of Reeds" (the site's Old Testament uses that name). The Greek translators called it the Erythra Thalassa, "Red Sea," the Greek name for the waters south and east of Egypt, including what we call the Red Sea and the Gulf of Suez. Stephen speaks Greek, so this translation keeps "the Red Sea" here, as in Hebrews 11:29. The topic page on the Sea of Reeds discusses where the crossing may have been.

a: a prophet for you from among your brothers, a prophet like me
p: Peter quoted the same promise (3:22). Stephen sets it in the middle of the story of Moses' rejection.
b: Moses had said: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers. You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). In the Old Testament this means the line of prophets God would keep sending. By Jesus' day many Jews looked for one final prophet like Moses (John 1:21; John 6:14), and a Qumran text, the Testimonia (4Q175), quotes this passage among its hopes. Peter applied it to Jesus (3:22–23). Stephen sets it right after describing how Israel pushed Moses away: the people who rejected the first deliverer would reject the second.

p: The Greek word is ekklēsia, the word for "church." Here it means Israel gathered at Sinai.
b: Stephen uses ekklēsia for Israel at Sinai, as the Greek Old Testament does for "the day of the assembly" (Deuteronomy 4:10; Deuteronomy 9:10; Deuteronomy 18:16). This translation follows the shared terms of the site: "assembly" for Israel in the wilderness, "church" for the Christian community (5:11). The same Greek word covers both, and readers have long seen the link: the gathering of Jesus' followers stands in the line of Israel gathered at Sinai to hear God's word.

p: Accused of speaking against the law, Stephen calls it God's living words given to Israel.
b: The charge was that Stephen never stopped speaking "against the law" (6:13). Here he calls what Moses received at Sinai logia zōnta, "living sayings" or "living oracles": words that come from the living God and give life (Deuteronomy 32:47; Leviticus 18:5). Logia is used of God's sayings in Romans 3:2. Stephen's complaint is not that the law was bad, but that Israel did not obey it (7:39, 53). Readers who think Stephen rejected the law and readers who think he upheld it both need to account for this phrase.

p: The Greek has a one-word verb, moschopoieō, "to make a calf." It is found nowhere before Acts.
b: Stephen tells the golden calf story (Exodus 32) with a coined word, emoschopoiēsan, "they calf-made." He adds that they celebrated "what their own hands had made," a phrase the prophets used to mock idols (Isaiah 2:8; Jeremiah 1:16). Keep it in mind: at 7:48 Stephen will say that the Most High does not live in what "hands have made." The calf was Israel's first attempt to have a god they could see and carry, and Stephen sets it beside the tent and the house.

a: handed them over to serve the army of heaven
p: God punished idolatry by letting Israel have what it wanted: other gods.
b: "The army of heaven" is the sun, moon and stars, which Israel was forbidden to worship (Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3) but did worship in the time of the kings (2 Kings 17:16; 2 Kings 21:3; Jeremiah 19:13). Stephen says God "handed them over," the same verb Paul uses three times in Romans 1:24–28 for God giving people over to what they chose. The punishment for the calf was more idolatry. "The book of the prophets" is the Twelve Prophets, Hosea to Malachi, which Jews copied as one scroll (compare Sirach 49:10).
r: Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3; 2 Kings 17:16; 2 Kings 21:3; Jeremiah 19:13; Romans 1:24–28; Sirach 49:10

a: You did not offer me slaughtered animals and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, did you, house of Israel?
p: Stephen quotes Amos as the Greek Old Testament has it. The Hebrew differs in several words.
b: Amos asked whether Israel brought God sacrifices in the wilderness (Amos 5:25). The Greek question expects the answer "no": the forty years were not a time of true worship. The next verse (7:43) follows the Greek of Amos 5:26–27 closely, and the Greek differs from the Hebrew: where the Hebrew names Sikkuth and Kiyyun (probably Assyrian star gods), the Greek has "the tent of Moloch" and "the star of the god Rephan," and where Amos says "beyond Damascus," Stephen says "beyond Babylon" (see 7:43).

p: The Greek Old Testament read the names in Amos 5:26 differently from the Hebrew. Stephen follows the Greek.
b: The Hebrew of Amos 5:26 reads sikkut malkekhem and kiyyun tsalmekhem, "Sikkuth your king" and "Kiyyun your image." Most scholars take Sikkuth and Kiyyun as names of Mesopotamian star gods; Kiyyun matches Kayamanu, an Akkadian name for Saturn. The Greek translators read sukkat, "tent of," and took malkekhem "your king" as Moloch, the god of child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21). "Rephan" (Byzantine "Remphan") is probably a form of Kaiwan or Kiyyun that changed as the name was copied; just how it changed is uncertain. Stephen's point stands either way: Israel carried a tent for false gods while it had the tent of the testimony (7:44).
orig: τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ Μολὸχ ... Ῥαιφάν (tēn skēnēn tou Moloch ... Raiphan)

p: Amos threatened exile "beyond Damascus." Stephen says "beyond Babylon."
b: In both the Hebrew and the Greek of Amos 5:27, God says he will deport Israel "beyond Damascus," which happened when Assyria took the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Stephen says "beyond Babylon." Most readers think he updates the prophecy to cover the later exile of Judah to Babylon in 586 BC, which his hearers knew as the great punishment of Jerusalem. Others see a slip of memory. Updating a prophecy to its fuller fulfillment was a normal Jewish way of reading Scripture, as the Qumran commentaries show; the Damascus Document reads this very passage of Amos in its own way (Damascus Document 7:14–15).

p: The Greek name of the tabernacle. Stephen says God gave its pattern. His complaint is not about the tent.
b: The Greek Old Testament often calls the tabernacle "the tent of the testimony" (Exodus 27:21; Numbers 17:7), where the Hebrew has "the tent of meeting." It held the tablets of the law, the "testimony." Stephen stresses that it was made exactly by the model God showed Moses: "See to it that you make them by their pattern, the one you are being shown on the mountain" (Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5 quotes it). The tent God designed contrasts with "Moloch's tent" (7:43), which Israel made. It was portable, going with the people from the wilderness into the land, which suits Stephen's picture of a God on the move.

p: The Greek name is Iēsous, the same name as Jesus. The KJV printed "Jesus" here.
b: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are one name: Iēsous, from Hebrew Yehoshua, "the LORD saves." The KJV kept "Jesus" here and in Hebrews 4:8, which confuses many readers; modern Bibles write "Joshua" where the Old Testament leader is meant. Some early Christians, such as Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 113), made much of the shared name, seeing Joshua, who led Israel into the land, as a picture of Jesus.

a: Solomon, though, built him a house
p: Readers disagree whether Stephen rejects the temple itself or only the belief that God can be contained in it.
b: Stephen contrasts David, who asked to find a dwelling for God, with Solomon, who built a house. Then "But" in 7:48. Against the temple: some, such as Marcel Simon, read Stephen as saying the temple was a mistake from the start, a departure from the movable tent God designed. Against a wrong view of it: others note that Solomon himself prayed, "But can God truly make his home on earth? Look: the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you. Then how could this house I built be enough!" (1 Kings 8:27). On this reading Stephen attacks the idea that God is bound to the building. A word play: in 2 Samuel 7, God refuses David's offer to build a house and promises to build David a "house," a dynasty, instead, fulfilled in Jesus. Luke's own Gospel and Acts show Jesus and the apostles honoring the temple (Luke 2:46–49; Acts 3:1), which counts against the strongest reading.

t: "Made by hands": the word for idols
p: In the Greek Old Testament, "handmade" is a word for idols. Applying it to the temple is shocking.
b: Cheiropoiētos, "made by hand," is the Greek Old Testament's word for idols (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 2:18; Isaiah 46:6). Stephen has just said Israel celebrated "what their own hands had made" at the calf (7:41). Now he uses the idol-word for the temple. Jesus' accusers said he would tear down the sanctuary "that human hands made" and build another "that no hands made" (Mark 14:58). Paul says the same of the God who made the world (17:24), and Hebrews of the true sanctuary (Hebrews 9:11, 24). To Stephen's hearers, putting the temple and idols in one breath would have sounded like blasphemy, which is why the speech ends as it does.
r: 7:41; 17:24; Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 2:18; Isaiah 46:6; Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11; Hebrews 9:24

a: Heaven is a throne for me, and the earth is a stool for my feet
p: Stephen's last Scripture is from the end of Isaiah, where God questions any house built for him.
b: Stephen quotes Isaiah 66:1–2 as the Greek has it, close to the Hebrew. The site's Isaiah reads the questions as, "Where is the place where I would rest?" (Isaiah 66:1) and "My hand made all these things" (Isaiah 66:2). Many scholars place this oracle among people rebuilding the temple after the exile; traditional readers assign it to Isaiah himself. Either way, the maker of heaven and earth cannot be housed, and what he looks for is "the poor one, stricken in spirit" (Isaiah 66:2), who trembles at God's word. Stephen stops before that line, but his hearers knew it. The prophet himself had said what Stephen is accused of saying.

a: Stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears
p: Every phrase Stephen uses here comes from Moses and the prophets.
b: "Stiff-necked" is God's own word for Israel after the golden calf: "you are a stiff-necked people" (Exodus 33:3; compare Exodus 33:5; Exodus 34:9). "Uncircumcised in heart" comes from the law and the prophets: "their uncircumcised heart" (Leviticus 26:41), "circumcise the foreskin of your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:16), and Jeremiah 9:26; "uncircumcised ears" is Jeremiah's phrase for ears that will not hear (Jeremiah 6:10). "Resisting the Holy Spirit" recalls Isaiah 63:10, where Israel "grieved his holy spirit" (Isaiah 63:10). Stephen does not invent an outsider's attack on Israel; he speaks as a Jewish prophet, in the words Israel's own Scriptures used to call Israel back.
r: 7:8; Exodus 33:3; Exodus 33:5; Leviticus 26:41; Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 6:10; Jeremiah 9:26; Isaiah 63:10

a: Was there one prophet your ancestors did not hound?
t: Killing the prophets: an inside critique
p: Israel's Scriptures told of prophets persecuted and killed. Stephen speaks within that tradition.
b: Nehemiah's great prayer confesses that Israel's ancestors killed the prophets sent to turn them back (Nehemiah 9:26), and Chronicles says the people mocked God's messengers until there was no remedy (2 Chronicles 36:16). Jewish tradition told of prophets' deaths: Isaiah sawn in two, Jeremiah stoned (Lives of the Prophets; Ascension of Isaiah). Jesus said the same: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killer of the prophets, stoner of those sent to her!" (Matthew 23:37). This is a Jew's charge against his own people's leaders, in a family argument. Later Christians turned such words into a charge against all Jews; Stephen's "your ancestors" here is spoken by a man who called the same ancestors "our ancestors" through the rest of the speech (7:11–45).
r: 7:11–45; 1 Kings 19:10; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Matthew 23:29–37; 1 Thessalonians 2:14–15

p: A title for Jesus in Acts. It recalls the righteous servant of Isaiah 53.
b: Peter called Jesus "the Holy and Righteous One" (3:14), and Ananias of Damascus will tell Paul he has seen "the Righteous One" (22:14). Isaiah's servant is "the righteous one, my servant," who "will make the many righteous" (Isaiah 53:11). The Wisdom of Solomon describes the ungodly plotting against the righteous man who calls himself God's child (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20), and 1 Enoch uses "the Righteous One" as a title of the coming judge. At Jesus' death Luke's centurion calls him righteous (Luke 23:47).
r: 3:14; 22:14; Isaiah 53:11; Wisdom of Solomon 2:12–20; 1 Enoch 38:2; Luke 23:47; 1 Peter 3:18; 1 John 2:1

p: Exodus does not mention angels at Sinai. Later Jewish and Christian writers said they were there.
b: Exodus 19–20 has God speak the Ten Words himself. But Deuteronomy says the LORD "came from among ten thousands of holy ones" (Deuteronomy 33:2), with a fiery law at his right hand, and the Greek of that verse says "angels with him at his right hand." By the first century many Jews believed angels took part in giving the law (Jubilees 1:27–29; Josephus, Antiquities 15.136, though the meaning there is debated). Stephen uses the belief to stress the law's glory: you received it by angels and still did not keep it. Paul and Hebrews use the same belief the other way, to set the law below Christ (Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). The Greek eis diatagas angelōn can mean "as ordained by angels" or "by orders of angels."

p: The verb literally means "to be sawn through." Luke used it in 5:33.
b: Diapriō means to saw in two. Used of the heart, it is rage that rips a person apart inside. It is the reaction of the council in 5:33 too. Compare 2:37, where Peter's words "pierced their hearts," a different verb, katanyssomai, and the hearers asked what to do. Both crowds are wounded by the word; one repents, one attacks. "Gnashing teeth" is the Psalms' picture of the wicked attacking the righteous: "they ground their teeth at me" (Psalm 35:16; compare Psalm 37:12; Job 16:9).

a: with Jesus standing at God's right hand
p: Elsewhere Jesus sits at God's right hand. Only here is he standing, and readers have offered several reasons.
b: Psalm 110:1 says "Sit at my right hand," and Jesus told the council that the Son of Man would be seated at the right hand of the Power (Luke 22:69; Matthew 26:64). Here, twice, he stands. Readings: to welcome Stephen, rising for the first martyr (an old and popular reading); as witness or advocate, standing in the heavenly court to speak for Stephen as he had promised to acknowledge those who acknowledge him (Luke 12:8); as judge, rising to judge those condemning Stephen (compare Isaiah 3:13, "he is on his feet to judge the peoples"); as priest, standing to serve. Some think the change carries no meaning. The witness or advocate reading fits the trial setting best, and many commentators prefer it.
r: 7:56; Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 3:13; Daniel 7:13–14; Matthew 26:64; Luke 12:8–9; Luke 22:69; Hebrews 10:11–12

t: "The Son of Man" from someone else's lips
p: Outside the Gospels, only Stephen calls Jesus "the Son of Man" with this title.
b: In the Gospels nearly every use of "the Son of Man" is on Jesus' own lips; the exceptions repeat his words, as when the crowd asks, "Who is this Son of Man?" (John 12:34), or the angels at the tomb remind the women of what he said (Luke 24:7). Outside the Gospels Stephen is the only one besides Jesus to use the full title, and the only believer anywhere who uses it to confess Jesus (Revelation 1:13 and Revelation 14:14 have only "one like a son of man"). The title comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes before God and receives everlasting rule. At his trial Jesus had told the council they would see the Son of Man at the right hand of power (Matthew 26:64). Now, before the same council, Stephen says he sees it.
r: Daniel 7:13–14; Matthew 26:64; Luke 22:69; Luke 24:7; John 12:34; Revelation 1:13; Revelation 14:14

a: with one mind they charged at him
p: The word Luke uses for the church's unity now describes the mob.
b: Homothymadon, "with one mind" or "all together," is one of Luke's favorite words for the church gathered in unity (1:14; 2:46; 4:24; 5:12). Here the council is of one mind in killing. Luke's irony is that unity is not good in itself: it depends on what people are united for. Holding their ears is a refusal to hear what they took as blasphemy, and the loud shout drowns it out.

a: They drove him out of the city and started stoning him
p: The law required stoning outside the camp, with the witnesses first. Luke's details match.
b: The law of Moses commanded that a blasphemer be taken "outside the camp" and stoned by the community (Leviticus 24:14), and that "The hands of the witnesses are to be first against him" (Deuteronomy 17:7). The Mishnah describes a stoning place outside the court and the witnesses taking the lead (Sanhedrin 6:1–4). Luke's witnesses take off their outer cloaks to have free arms. Christian tradition placed the site north of the Damascus Gate (a basilica was built there in the 400s), while a later tradition put it east of the city near the gate now called St Stephen's Gate. Like Jesus, Stephen dies outside the city (Hebrews 13:12).

a: a young man whose name was Saul
p: Luke's first mention of Paul is as a bystander at Stephen's death.
b: The Greek neanias was used for men from about twenty to forty, so Saul need not have been a boy. He holds the witnesses' cloaks, which some read as a sign that he was in charge, and 8:1 says he agreed with the killing. Paul himself later remembers this day: "When they were spilling the blood of Stephen, your witness, I was right there. I stood by, I agreed with it, and I kept watch over the cloaks of the men who were killing him" (22:20). A line often credited to Augustine, from a sermon on Stephen (Sermon 382) whose authorship is doubted, says that if Stephen had not prayed, the church would not have had Paul; the thought became a commonplace in preaching on this chapter.

a: as he called out in prayer
p: Stephen "calls" on Jesus as Israel called on the LORD. The KJV supplied "God" here, in italics.
b: The verb epikaleomai is the Greek Old Testament's word for calling on the name of the LORD in prayer (Genesis 4:26; Joel 2:32). Peter quoted Joel at Pentecost: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (2:21). Stephen calls on "Lord Jesus." The Greek has no object for the verb, and the KJV printed "calling upon God," in italics to show the word was supplied; the prayer that follows is addressed to Jesus.

p: Jesus on the cross gave his spirit to the Father. Stephen gives his to Jesus.
b: Jesus' last words in Luke are the words of the psalm, "Into your hand I place my spirit" (Psalm 31:5), addressed to the Father (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays the same kind of prayer, but to Jesus. Historians of early Christianity, such as Larry Hurtado, point to this as early evidence that Jesus' followers prayed to him as they prayed to God. The parallels with Jesus' death run through the scene: false witnesses, a temple charge, the Son of Man at God's right hand, a prayer committing his spirit, and a prayer for his killers (7:60). Luke tells the first martyr's death as a reflection of his Lord's.

a: Lord, do not count this sin against them!
p: Stephen's prayer echoes Jesus' prayer from the cross, "Father, forgive them."
b: In Luke 23:34 Jesus prays that the Father will forgive his executioners, because they do not know what they are doing. That prayer is missing from some very old manuscripts of Luke (P75, Vaticanus, the first hand of Bezae), and scholars debate whether it is original; Stephen's prayer here is often cited on both sides, as proof that Luke knew it or as the model a scribe borrowed. Either way, Stephen does what Jesus taught, to pray for those who mistreat you (Luke 6:28). The verb "count against" (histēmi, "set, place") is a bookkeeping picture: do not enter this sin on their account.

p: A gentle word for a violent death. The New Testament often calls the death of believers sleep.
b: Koimaomai, "fall asleep," was a common way to speak of death, Jewish and Greek, and Christians made it their own because they expected to wake in the resurrection (John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–16; 1 Corinthians 15:20). Luke ends the stoning with this word: after stones and shouting, quiet. Whether "sleep" means the dead are unconscious until the resurrection is a question on which the churches differ; the Where Christians differ card at John 11 sets out their answers. Stephen's own prayer, "welcome my spirit" (7:59), is often cited in that discussion.
